title: Given a binary tree, find its diameter, defined as the number of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The path may or may not pass through the root. Explain why a single post-order traversal that returns subtree heights while updating a global maximum is the efficient solution.
shortTitle: Tree Diameter (Longest Path Between Any Two Nodes)

s1_definition.profdef: Tree Diameter is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the longest path between any two nodes, where the path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal where each node returns its height to its parent while simultaneously updating a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which equals the left height plus the right height plus one node. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree, and management wants the longest possible escalation path between any two desks, the two desks that are farthest apart in the chain of command. That longest stretch might not go through the head office at all; it could run up one branch and down another. We measure, at every desk, how deep its left reports and right reports go, and the widest span through that desk is a candidate for the longest stretch overall.
s1_definition.oneliner: Post-order return each subtree's height, and at every node update the best diameter as left height plus right height plus one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tree Diameter is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the longest path between any two nodes, where the path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal where each node returns its height to its parent while simultaneously updating a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which equals the left height plus the right height plus one node. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree, and management wants the longest possible escalation path between any two desks, the two desks that are farthest apart in the chain of command. That longest stretch might not go through the head office at all; it could run up one branch and down another. We measure, at every desk, how deep its left reports and right reports go, and the widest span through that desk is a candidate for the longest stretch overall.

**One line to remember:** Post-order return each subtree's height, and at every node update the best diameter as left height plus right height plus one.

sections.s2_technical:
The key realization is that the longest path through a particular node uses the deepest path going down its left child and the deepest path going down its right child, joined at the node. So if we know the height of the left subtree and the height of the right subtree, the candidate diameter centered at this node is `leftHeight + rightHeight + 1` counted in nodes. We keep a shared maximum and update it at every node, for example `maxDiameter = Math.max(maxDiameter, leftHeight + rightHeight + 1);`.

The same traversal must also return a height to the parent, so the recursion returns `Math.max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1`. A null child returns height zero. This dual role, updating a global while returning a local value, is what makes it a single linear pass rather than recomputing heights repeatedly.

A senior-level nuance is the counting convention. Some definitions count the diameter in edges rather than nodes; in nodes it is left height plus right height plus one, and in edges it is left height plus right height. I state the convention explicitly so the off-by-one is deliberate. Another nuance is that the naive approach of computing height independently at every node is O(n²); folding the height return into the same traversal removes the repeated work.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to understand the longest escalation chain in its approval hierarchy, the greatest distance between any two desks, because a very long chain slows down approvals and signals an over-deep structure. The longest chain might run entirely within two sub-branches and never touch the head office. This is exactly how Tree Diameter works: the farthest two desks define the diameter, wherever they sit.

Problem 2 — Measuring each desk's depth over and over would be slow for a large hierarchy. This is why a single post-order pass returns each subtree's depth to its parent while updating the running longest-span, so every desk is measured once.

The code defines a `DeskNode`. A `TreeDiameterService` exposes `longestEscalationChain(root)` returning the diameter in nodes. A `Demo` builds a hierarchy whose longest chain does not pass through the root and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Head with left Regional and right Audit; Regional with left Zone and right Branch; Zone with left Terminal.

Step 1: Post-order starts at the deepest leaves. Terminal has no children, returns height 1, candidate through Terminal is 0 + 0 + 1 = 1.

Step 2: Zone has left Terminal (height 1) and no right. Candidate through Zone is 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. Zone returns max(1,0)+1 = 2.

Step 3: Branch is a leaf, returns 1, candidate 1. Regional has left Zone (height 2) and right Branch (height 1). Candidate through Regional is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, a new maximum. Regional returns max(2,1)+1 = 3.

Step 4: Audit is a leaf, returns 1. Head has left Regional (height 3) and right Audit (height 1). Candidate through Head is 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, a new maximum.

Step 5: Final diameter is 5 nodes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tree Diameter finds the longest path between any two nodes in a binary tree, and crucially that path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal that does two jobs at once. For each node I recursively compute the height of its left and right subtrees, then I update a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which is the left height plus the right height plus one node. The same call returns the node's own height to its parent, which is the deeper of the two child heights plus one.

The nuance I always state explicitly is the counting convention. Counting the diameter in nodes gives left height plus right height plus one; counting in edges gives left height plus right height. I announce which convention I am using so the plus-one is a deliberate decision rather than an accidental off-by-one. I also point out that computing height independently at every node would be quadratic, and folding the height return into the diameter pass is what keeps the algorithm linear.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to analyse the approval hierarchy, where management wanted the longest escalation chain between any two desks because an over-long chain slows approvals, and that chain often ran across two sub-branches without touching the head office. I ran one post-order pass that returned each subtree's depth while updating the longest span through each desk, and reported the diameter to the org-structure dashboard. Explaining the dual role of the single traversal, returning a height while updating a global maximum, is what shows an interviewer that I can turn a tempting quadratic solution into a clean linear one.
